summary: Learners treat angle measure as additive (a whole angle equals the sum of its non-overlapping parts, CCSS 4.MD.7) and turn an angle diagram into an equation with a symbol for the unknown, then solve by subtraction. The disciplined routine is: read the configuration to fix the whole (straight line = 180°, point = 360°, or a decomposition whole that is either named or found by adding the parts), write the equation, solve, and sanity-check the answer against the diagram. The diagram supplies given facts from its marked values; it is not to be remeasured with a protractor, and it may be drawn not to scale.
misconceptions: Subtracts from the wrong whole — uses 180° at a point or 360° on a straight line because the configuration was not identified first.
Treats angle measure as non-additive — tries to measure the unknown on the diagram instead of computing it from the others.
Reads the diagram as if it were to scale — assumes two angles that 'look equal' are equal (e.g. an isosceles-looking triangle), or measures the printed unknown, rather than using the marked values.
Arithmetic slip when subtracting from 180°/360° (e.g. 180 − 145 gives 45 instead of 35) — the angle reasoning is sound but the subtraction fails.

activities.title: Name the whole, then build and solve the equation
steps: Look at each diagram and first decide and state the whole before any arithmetic: a straight line split by a ray is a half turn (180°); angles meeting at a point make a whole turn (360°); for a decomposed angle, either the whole is named and you find a missing part, or the parts are marked and you add them to find the whole.
For a straight line with one angle marked 65° and the other marked x, write the equation 65 + x = 180, then solve to get x = 115°.
For angles round a point marked 120°, 90° and x, write 120 + 90 + x = 360, then solve to get x = 150°.
For a large angle decomposed into two marked parts, 35° and 40°, write 35 + 40 = w with a symbol for the whole, then solve to get w = 75°.
After solving, check the answer back against the fixed whole (do all the parts add to 180° or 360°, or to the stated decomposition whole?).
activities.insight: An unknown angle is determined by the marked angles and the fixed whole, so it can be computed with an equation rather than measured. Choosing the correct whole (180° vs 360° vs a decomposition whole) is the first decision, not an afterthought.

activities.title: Part-whole bar model linking the symbol to the shared whole
steps: Draw or use a bar representing the fixed whole (e.g. a bar labelled 180° for a straight line, or 360° for a point).
Fill the bar with the known angles as labelled segments, leaving a gap for the unknown.
Label the remaining gap as x, and read off that x is what is left when the known parts are taken from the whole.
Connect this to the equation: the gap in the bar is 180 − 65, which is the same as solving 65 + x = 180.
Optionally, use a live model where solving the subtraction makes the x segment snap to exactly fill the bar, so the 'parts complete the whole' idea is visible.
activities.insight: The algebraic symbol x corresponds to a concrete missing segment of a fixed shared whole; subtraction finds the gap that completes the whole.

activities.title: Decompose and recombine a concrete angle
steps: Take a concrete angle (e.g. a cut paper wedge, or an angle built from two strips) and split it into two marked parts.
Add the two parts to confirm they equal the whole angle (e.g. 35° + 40° = 75°).
Reverse the process: cover one part and find it by subtracting the known part from the whole.
State in words that non-overlapping parts that exactly fill the angle always sum to the whole, so a missing part can be computed rather than measured.
Note that the paper wedge or strips are physical approximations with slight thickness; the mathematical angle being reasoned about is the idealised figure they represent.
activities.insight: Angle measure is additive: parts sum to the whole, and reversing this gives a missing part by subtraction. This directly addresses the belief that an unknown angle must be measured.

activities.title: Not-to-scale diagram: reason from marked values, not appearance
steps: Work a diagram labelled 'not drawn to scale' where the printed unknown angle looks smaller than the given 65° angle (for example, drawn acute) but must still equal 115° by the rule.
Cover the figure and solve from the marked numbers and the fixed whole alone (65 + x = 180, x = 115°).
Only then reveal the drawing and notice the picture was misleading.
Discuss a case where two angles 'look equal' but are not marked equal, and explain why you cannot assume equality from appearance.
activities.insight: A diagram carries stated facts, not scale: answers come from the marked values and the rule, not from measuring the printed figure or assuming look-alike angles are equal.

activities.title: Mixed practice: choose the whole each time
steps: Work a mixed set that includes a straight-line single-unknown case, a point case with several angles and one unknown, and a decomposition case (adding two marked parts to find the whole, e.g. 35 + 40 = 75°, or finding a missing part from a named whole).
For each item, write the equation first, labelling the whole, before giving a number.
Try writing the same relationship two ways for one diagram, e.g. 65 + x = 180 and x = 180 − 65, to show they describe the same additive structure.

Sanity-check each result: plug the answer back and confirm the parts add to the stated whole (e.g. for two 100° angles and x at a point, 100 + 100 + 160 = 360); ask whether the answer is even possible (e.g. a result of 180° or more for one of two angles on a straight line, or a zero or negative result, means the whole or a value was misread).
activities.insight: Fluency means choosing the correct whole for each configuration rather than applying one habitual routine, and verifying the answer against the fixed whole.

checkQuestion: Put three diagrams in front of the child. (1) A straight line split by one ray, one angle marked 65°, the other x. (2) Angles round a point marked 120°, 90° and x. (3) A large angle decomposed into two marked parts, 35° and 40°, asking for the whole. Say: 'Find each unknown, and write down the equation you used to get it.' Make diagram (1) deliberately NOT to scale so the printed x looks bigger than 65°. Watch how they set up and solve — do not prompt the rule.
checkAnswer: (1) writes 65 + x = 180 and solves x = 115°; (2) writes 120 + 90 + x = 360 and solves x = 150°; (3) writes 35 + 40 = 75°. Uses the marked values and the correct whole for each configuration, and does NOT try to measure the printed (not-to-scale) angle.
